1.x: The tension between Jesus and the religious establishment reaches a breaking point over the interpretation of the Sabbath. Under the Law of Moses, it was actually legal to pluck a neighbor’s grain by hand as you walked through their field to satisfy immediate hunger (Deut 23:25).

2.x: The Pharisees observed the disciples performing four specific actions that had been categorized as “work” in their oral tradition (as preserved in the Mishnah): (1) Reaping: Plucking the heads of grain; (2) Threshing: Rubbing the grain in their hands to remove the hunks. (3) Winnowing: Separating the chaff from the grain; (4) Preparing food: The act of getting the grain ready to eat. The Pharisees believed that protecting the sanctity of the Sabbath was the ultimate sign of devotion to God. To them, the Law was a fence designed to keep Israel holy. By “working” to feed themselves, the disciples were, in the eyes of the Pharisees, breaking one of the Ten Commandments. They truly believed that Jesus was leading his followers into sin by ignoring these traditional boundaries. Jesus did not follow “oral traditions.”

5.x: “have ye not read”: Again, the expectation is that they were familiar with God’s Word after having read it. Jesus moves from a historical example to a legal one. He points out that the priests in the Temple technically “break” the Sabbath every week by performing the heavy physical labor of animal sacrifice, cleaning, and lighting fires. The Law commands rest, yet the Law also commands the priests to work on the Sabbath. The logic is that the service of the Temple is a higher “duty” that supersedes the individual Sabbath day, hence they are blameless before the Law.

6.x: Jesus then makes a bold claim: “I say unto you, That in this place is one greater than the temple”. If the higher duty of the Temple justifies the priests working on the Sabbath, then the even higher duty of Jesus justifies his disciple’s actions. Christ’s human body is the true temple (Jn 2:21).

7.x: Jesus concludes by citing Hosea 6:6. “Sacrifice” represents the outward, formal, and ritualistic requirements of religion (the “literal” keeping of rules). “Mercy” represents the heart of God: compassion, kindness, and the well-being of others. Jesus tells the Pharisees that if they truly understood God’s heart, they “would not have condemned the guiltless.” He is essentially saying that they have used the Law as a weapon to hurt people rather than a tool to honor God.

8.x: This passage is the “proof text” for why the literal Sabbath is not a binding requirement for those in Christ: (1) David was justified because of his relationship to God’s mission; (2) The Priests were justified because of their service to God’s house; (3) The disciples are justified because they are with the Lord of the Sabbath. If you are “in Christ,” you are in the presence of the one who is greater than the Temple and greater than the Sabbath day. Therefore, your “rest” is found in your relationship with Him, not in your ability to follow a checklist of “dos and don’ts” on a Saturday. By claiming to be “Lord” (Kyrios) of the Sabbath, Jesus was making a claim to deity: only the one who instituted the Sabbath has the authority to oversee or change its application. If God rested on the seventh day and commanded its observance, then only God can claim to be its Master. Jesus is telling the Pharisees that they have misplaced their worship. They were worshipping the DAY, but the DESIGNER of the Day was standing right in front of them. If Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, then the Sabbath must bow to His purposes. His purpose is the restoration and “rest” of humanity. In Galatians, Paul describes the Law as a tutor meant to lead us to Christ. Once the “Lord of the Sabbath” arrived, the tutor’s job of enforcing a specific day was finished. Because the Lord of the Sabbath lives within the believer, the believer is always “in” the Sabbath. You don’t have to wait for Friday sundown to experience God’s rest; you possess it because you possess the Lord of that day.

** As a Oneness Christian, we believe that the “Son of Man” (the singular masculine God manifested in the man Jesus) is the same “Father” (the eternal Spirit) who rested on the seventh day in Genesis. This verse proves that Jesus is the God of the OT. When Jesus says he is “Lord of the Sabbath,” he is declaring that He is the One who spoke to Moses on Sinai. Therefore, if the Lawgiver is now present in the flesh, He has the absolute right to fulfill the Sabbath and offer Himself as the “rest” for our souls, moving us from a literal day to a spiritual reality.

9.x: Jews gathered in synagogues on the Sabbath for worship, prayer, Torah reading, and teaching. This was a central practice in Second Temple Judaism and continues today. Jesus’ custom was to attend synagogue on the Sabbath (Lk 4:16), where he taught; Paul reasoned there every Sabbath as well (Acts 13:14-15; 17:2). These gatherings involved Scripture readings, psalms, and communal prayer. Synagogues were not established by God, yet Jesus accepted them. They emerged during the Babylonian exile as local worship centers supplementing the Temple. By NT times, weekly Sabbath services were standard, fostering community amid dispersion.

10.x: Jesus enters the synagogue and encounters a man with a “withered hand.” The Pharisees, looking for a reason to accuse him, ask: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath days?” In their legal code (the Mishnah), healing was only permitted on the Sabbath if a person’s life was in immediate danger. Since a withered hand was a chronic condition and not life-threatening, they viewed healing it as “work.”

17.x: Matthew quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 to explain why Jesus withdrew quietly rather than engaging in a political fight with the Pharisees.

18.x: The man Jesus is identified by Matthew as the “Servant of the LORD(YHWH).” And we know that this human servant is also God’s only begotten Son born of Mary. This sinless servant served YHWH as the perfect instrument of redemption. “I will put my Spirit upon him”: The "putting of the Spirit upon Him" is the biblical way of describing God’s presence fully inhabiting the life of the human Jesus. The man Jesus was indwelt by the Spirit of God Himself: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” (Col 2:9 KJV); “Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost(the Spirit of YHWH)” (Lk 4:1). “God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself (2 Cor 5:19 KJV). This servant, “being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil 2:8 KJV). YHWH gave His servant access to the Spirit “without limit” (Jn 3:34 BSB), and “exalted him” and gave him “a name which is above EVERY NAME” (Phil 2:9 KJV). The name is Jesus(which means YHWH-saves): “Holy Father, keep them in Your name(Jesus), the name which You have given Me(Jesus)” (Jn 17:11 BSB). The glorified servant is what we will see on the Throne under one face and under one name, Jesus (Rev 22:3-4; Isa 6:1; Jn 12:41). “..shall shew judgement to the Gentiles”: The Servant of the LORD will reveal God’s justice in law and the gospel.
The Trinitarian view of this has the 1st divine person of the Trinity send the 3rd person of the Trinity to indwell the 2nd person of the Trinity.

19.x: This verse describes the specific method and temperament of Jesus. “He shall not strive(quarrel)”: The Greek word for strive/quarrel is “erisei”, which refers to the kind of loud, angry debating or verbal strife that was very common among the religious schools of that day. While the Pharisees were “conspiring” (v14) and looking for a fight, Jesus refused to be a political agitator. He didn’t come to win arguments, he came to win souls. “Nor cry”: This refers to “shouting” or “clamoring.” In the ancient world, kings and conquerors entered cities with great fanfare, shouting their victories and demanding attention. Jesus’ authority didn’t rely on volume. His power was demonstrated through quiet healings and private restoration, not through self-promotion or demanding to be the center of a spectacle. “neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets”: This doesn’t mean Jesus never spoke in public (we know he preached to thousands). Rather it means he didn’t use the “streets” as a stage for self-advertisement or political grandstanding. He worked on individuals rather than playing the crowds. Jesus as our true “rest”, doesn’t come with loud legalism that demands performance and shouts: “Do more!”. Jesus’ “rest” does not “strive” or “quarrel” with your conscience about whether you’ve done enough, because we know that ultimately it is His works, not ours. The eternal Sprit (YHWH, the Father) didn’t come as a terrifying, booming voice from heaven like He did at Mount Sinai. Instead, He came as a man (a servant) who was approachable and humble.

20.x: This verse describes how Jesus treats the “spiritually exhausted.” Jesus uses two metaphors to describe people who are at their absolute breaking point: (1) The Bruised Reed: In the ancient world, reeds were used as measuring rods or musical pipes. If a reed was bruised or cracked, it was useless. Most people would simply snap it off and throw it away. (2) The Smoking Flax: This refers to the flax wick of an oil lamp (the cord on a candle made of flax that uses capillary action to draw fuel (liquid wax, oil, or fuel) up to a flame in candles, oil lamps, or stoves)..When the oil runs dry, the flame dies down to a flicker, producing more irritating smoke than light. Usually, you would pinch it out and replace it. Jesus is saying that he does not discard “useless” or failing” people. While the religious leaders (the Pharisees) would “break” a person with more rules or “extinguish” them with judgement, Jesus restores them. He is the one who binds up the bruise and adds the “oil” of the Spirit to the dying flame. “Till he send forth judgement unto victory”: When we hear “justice,” we often think of retribution (punishing the bad guys) or legalism. However, the Greek word used here (krisis) and the Hebrew context it draws from (Isa 42) point toward restorative justice. In this context, justice means setting things right. It is the alignment of the world with God’s original intent. If a reed is bruised, “justice” is not breaking it further; justice is healing it so it can be a reed again. The “victory” is when the “quiet” and “gentle” way of the Messiah overcomes the “crushing” ways of the world. Justice here refers to the defense of the weak. While the world’s systems often trample the “bruised reeds,” the justice of the Messiah ensures they are protected and given a place of honor. While the Pharisees were awaiting a “Crushing King” who would bring justice through a sword, Matthew points out that the true Messiah brings justice through tenderness. The “Justice” is the radical idea that true power is found in the refusal to crush the weak. It is a promise that God’s ultimate triumph will be characterized by healing rather than destruction.

21.x: This is a massive shift. Up until this point, the Sabbath and the Law were specifically for Israel. By quoting this, Matthew is declaring that the Law is not the end goal. The goal is a Name (Jesus). The “gentiles” (the non-Jewish nations) will find their hope and their Sabbath rest in Jesus, not in a Jewish calendar. The Name of Jesus is the only name given to men for salvation (Acts 4:12). It is the name above every name (Phil 2:9). It is the name of the Father (Isa 9:6; Mt 1:21; Heb 1:4; 2:12; Jn 5:43; 10:25; 17:6; 17:11-12 BSB; 17:26). It is the supreme revelation of God’s character and power as YHWH-saves. The “trust” of the nations isn’t in a doctrine or a day of rest, but in the specific, saving Name of Jesus, which carries the full authority of the Father (the same YHWH of the OT).

24.x: The Pharisees could not deny the fact of the miracle (the man was clearly healed), so they attacked the source. By attributing Jesus’ power to “Beelzebub” (a name derived from a Philistine god, meaning “lord of the flies” or “lord of dung”), they were essentially calling the Holy Spirit a demon.

28.x: If the healing happened by the Spirit of God, it means the “Kingdom” is a present reality standing right in front of them. The parallel passage in Luke 11:20 shows Jesus casting out demons by the “finger of God.” The “Spirit of God” is the Father. Jesus is not a “second person” using a “third person”, rather the one God (the Spirit) is acting through the human vessel of the Son.

29.x: Jesus uses a “Strong Man” illustration to explain the miracle of the healed mute man. The Strong Man represents Satan. He has a “house” (the realm of darkness/sin) and “goods” (human souls held in bondage, like the man who was blind and mute). The Binder is Jesus. Before Jesus can “plunder” the house (heal and deliver people), he must first “bind” the power of the devil. The spoiling (plundering) is every miracle Jesus performs, which is a legal seizure. He is reclaiming human lives from the grip of the enemy.

30.x: There is no middle ground in the spiritual war. If you are not actively “with” Jeus, you are “against” him. Then he uses agricultural imagery. A shepherd gathers sheep; a wolf scatters them. By accursing Jesus of being demonic, the Pharisees were “scattering”, they were driving people away from the only one who could provide them with true “rest.”

33.x: Jesus is arguing that actions are merely the evidence of one’s inner nature. You cannot have a healthy tree producing rotten fruit, not a diseased tree producing delicious fruit. The Tree represents the heart or the inner nature of the person. The Fruit represents the words and actions of that person. The Pharisees were claiming to be servants of God (a “good tree”), yet their words toward Jesus were hateful and blasphemous (“corrupt fruit”). Jesus is exposing their inconsistency: their behavior proves that their “root” or heart is not right with God, regardless of how much they claim to follow the Law. This relates back to how salvation works. Salvation is by faith (the inner heart and nature of the tree), and not by works (the fruits that reflect the nature of the tree): “For by grace are ye saved through faith(the nature of the heart of the tree); and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works(not based on fruits), lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:8-9 KJV). Even James (who encourages works), he is always putting the FAITH under test, not the works: “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone” (Js 2:17 KJV). A “saving faith” will always come with works that give evidence of the genuineness of the faith, for “faith” is simply “acting as if it were true.” The capital sin is to believe that we earn salvation by our own “goodness”: “Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are FALLEN FROM GRACE.” (Gal 5:4 KJV).

Catholicism condemns salvation by faith alone: (Session 6, Canon IX) states: "If any one saith, that by faith alone the impious is justified; in such wise as to mean, that nothing else is required to CO-OPERATE in order TO THE OBTAINING THE GRACE OF JUSTIFICATION, and that it is not in any way necessary, that he be prepared and disposed by the movement of his own will; let him be ANATHEMA." This targets sola fide views denying free will's role or sacraments, not pure trust in Christ. Trent affirms INITIAL justification by grace through faith (Canon 1), but insists ongoing sanctification involves works (James 2:24). To break this down, first, let’s clarify the verse that they always cite: “YE SEE(not God) then how that by works a man is justified(vindicated), and not by faith only.” (Js 2:24 KJV). Notice the ones “seeing” in this verse are humans. Humans are the ones that know the nature of the tree by looking at the fruits (since they can’t see the interior). However, this is not what God sees: “For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; BUT NOT BEFORE GOD. For what saith the scripture? Abraham BELIEVED God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness. Now TO HIM THAT WORKETH is THE REWARD NOT reckoned OF GRACE, BUT OF DEBT. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, HIS FAITH is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4: 2-5 KJV). God is not impressed by our works. The Catholic idea that we can cooperate “in order to obtain the grace of justification” completely contradicts Scripture. By definition “grace” is not something you can earn. “But we are all as an unclean thing, and ALL OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS ARE AS FILTHY RAGS..” (Isa 64:6 KJV). The idea that we can “earn the grace of Justification” by our works is actually a capital sin (Gal 5:4): “And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then it is no more grace: otherwise work is no more work.” (Rom 11:6 KJV); “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us..” (Tit 3:5 KJV); “Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.” (Rom 4:4-5 KJV); “Who hath saved us… not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace…” (2 Tim 1:9 KJV); “Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ…” (Gal 2:16 KJV); “Where is boasting then? It is excluded… Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.” (Rom 3:27-28 KJV). ANY good work that we do, comes not from us, but from Christ. They are works that he prepared BEFORE THE FOUNDATION OF THE WORLD: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, so that no one may boast. For we are His workmanship, CREATED in Christ Jesus FOR GOOD WORKS, WHICH GOD PREPARED BEFOREHAND so that we should walk in them.” (Eph 2:8-10 BSB). Anyone who tries to defend that Catholicism does not teach salvation by works, needs to try to explain the “Treasury of Merit” that they invented in the Medieval period (11-12th centuries). Catholic theologians like Thomas Aquinas (1223-1274AC) began to teach that the saints’ works , united to Christ, have value for others. But the official statement came from Pope Clement VI (1343), in his papal bull Unigenitus Dei Filius, where he formally describes a “treasury of the Church,” which consists of the infinite merits of Christ AND the merits of the saints. Today, the Catechism states: “In the communion of saints, ‘a perennial link of charity exists between the faithful who have already reached their heavenly home, those who are expiating their sins in purgatory and those who are still pilgrims on earth. Between them there is, too, an abundant exchange of all good things.’ In this wonderful exchange, THE HOLINESS OF ONE PROFITS OTHERS, well beyond the harm that the sin of one could cause others. Thus recourse to the communion of saints LETS THE CONTRITE SINNER be more promptly and efficaciously PURIFIED OF THE PUNISHMENT FOR SIN.” (CCC 1475) & "THIS TREASURY INCLUDES AS WELL THE PRAYERS AND GOOD WORKS OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. They are truly immense, unfathomable, and even pristine in their value before God. IN THE TREASURY, TOO, ARE THE PRAYERS AND GOOD WORKS OF ALL THE SAINTS, all those who have followed in the footsteps of Christ the Lord and by his grace have made their lives holy and carried out the mission in the unity of the Mystical Body" (CCC 1477). Literally saying that the works of Mary and the Saints HELP IN PURIFYING OUR PUNISHMENT FOR SIN. Biblically speaking, that is blasphemy. But it doesn’t end there: “An indulgence is obtained through the Church who, by virtue of the power of binding and loosing granted her by Christ Jesus, intervenes in favor of individual Christians and OPENS FOR THEM THE TREASURY OF THE MERITS of Christ AND THE SAINTS TO OBTAIN FROM THE FATHER of mercies THE REMISSION OF THE TEMPORAL PUNISHMENTS DUE FOR THEIR SINS” (CCC 1478) & “Since the faithful departed now being purified are also members of the same communion of saints, one way WE CAN HELP THEM is to obtain indulgences for them, SO THAT THE TEMPORAL PUNISHMENT DUE FOR THEIR SINS MAY BE REMITTED” (CCC 1479). The Catholic Church is essentially saying that the merits of Mary and the Saints also help in obtaining mercy from the Father for the remission of our temporal punishment of our sin. The Bible says otherwise: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). Only Jesus has something to show for before the Father. Only Jesus has a sinless sacrifice to show for before the Father. No saint, nor Mary, nor any earthly men have ANYTHING to show for before the Father for our sins. It is the blood of Jesus on cavalry: “By the which will we are SANCTIFIED through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ ONCE FOR ALL” (Heb 10:10 KJV). “The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us FROM ALL SIN” (1 Jn 1:7 KJV). “In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins…” (Eph 1:7 KJV); “Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be SAVED FROM WRATH THROUGH HIM” (Rom 5:9 KJV). We are forgiven and sanctified through the work of Jesus Christ alone. Our works do not contribute to our salvation. Is that not fair? Well, thankfully it’s not fair, otherwise we’d all deserve death. That’s why salvation is by “grace”, aka a gift: “Therefore as by the offence of one(Adam) judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one(Jesus) the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life” (Rom 5:18-19 KJV). “For by one offering he hath PERFECTED FOR EVER them that are sanctified.” (Heb 10:14 KJV); “The chastisement of our peace was upon him…” (Isa 53:5 KJV) - the “chastisement” (punishment that brings peace) falls on Christ, not on Purgatory. “God was in Christ… not imputing their trespasses unto them…” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV) - if sins are not counted, THERE IS NO DEBT LEFT TO PAY. “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree…” (1 Pet 2:24 KJV) - Christ himself bore the penalty, not partially, BUT FULLY. “…having forgiven you all trespasses; Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us… nailing it to his cross.” (Col 2:13-14 KJV) - All trespasses, nothing left unpaid. Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin.” (Heb 10:17-18 KJV) - if no further offering is needed, no further payment remains. “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” - freely, not something we pay back later or through fire in purgatory. This is why Jesus told the thief on the cross (who had so much temporal punishment to burn off in purgatory): “TODAY (not after years of burning in purgatory) shalt thou be with me in paradise” (Lk 23:43 KJV).

34.x: Jesus’ harshest words are always aimed at the religious establishment. Having established that a tree is known by its fruit, he directly addresses the Pharisees, explaining that their venomous words are the natural overflow of their internal state. Jesus reveals that the mouth is essentially a “leak” for the heart. You cannot consistently hide what is inside. The Pharisee’s legalistic obsession with the Sabbath (outward) was a mask for a heart full of “poison” (the inward).

35.x: Jesus views the heart as a thesaurus (a treasure house or storehouse). Every thought and motive is stored there. If the “inventory” is evil, the “output” will be evil.

36.x: An “idle” (argos) word is one that is careless, lazy, or useless. Jessu warns that even the things we say when we think no one is listening (our casual criticisms or religious posturing) will be audited by God.

37.x: Words serve as the primary evidence in God’s courtroom. They reveal whether a person has truly accepted the “rest” and grace of God or is still operating out of a corrupt, legalistic heart. The takeaway here is that the only way to have a “good treasure” in the heart is through the infilling of the Holy Spirit. Without the Spirit of God, the human heart is naturally a “brood of vipers.” Salvation isn’t about “trying harder”, it’s about a total heart transplant that changes what you “store” inside.

3-4.x: “have ye not read”: Jesus expects his followers to read God’s Word. Jesus does not challenge the Sabbath law itself but the Pharisee’s interpretation of it. He reminds the Pharisees of an event from 1 Samuel 21, when David and his men were fleeing from King Saul. Being famished, David entered the house of God and ate the Bread of the Presence (the showbread). According to Levitical law (Lev 24:5-9), this bread was considered holy and was strictly reserved for the priests. Jesus points out that God did not strike David down for this. Why? Because the ritual requirement of “who eats the bread” was secondary to the immediate, life-preserving need of God’s anointed servant.

11-12.x: Jesus exposes their hypocrisy with a simple illustration. If one of the Pharisees had a sheep fall into a pit on the Sabbath, they would immediately pull it out to protect their financial investment, so Jesus argues that a human being is of much greater value than a sheep. “Wherefore it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days”: Jesus correctly interprets the Law of the Sabbath from “doing nothing” to “doing good.” He argues that failing to help someone when you have the power to do so is actually a greater violation of God’s heart than performing the “work” of healing.

13-14.x: Jesus heals the man. But “the Pharisees went out, and held a council against him, how they might destroy him.” This is the height of irony. While they were angry at Jesus for “working” to save a hand, they were perfectly willing to “work” on the Sabbath to plot a murder.

Luke’s parallel passage appears to distinguish two different Sabbath’s, one in which the disciples plucked grain, and a different Sabbath in which Jesus healed the man with a shriveled hand. Matthew 12:1-8 shows Jesus’ disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath, and in Matthew 12:9-14 it says: "And when he was departed thence, he went into their synagogue..." (KJV). Matthew does not explicitly say it was a different Sabbath. The narrative flows directly into the healing of the man with the withered hand. By contrast Luke 6:1-5 shows the grain-plucking incident and Luke 6:6-11 says: "And it came to pass also ON ANOTHER sabbath, that he entered into the synagogue and taught: and there was a man whose right hand was withered." (KJV). This is not a contradiction to what Matthew said. Matthew often compresses events together without indicating the amount of time between them. His phrase: “And when he was departed thence..” simply means Jesus left the grainfield and later entered a synagogue. It DOES NOT explicitly say this happened immediately or on the same Sabbath. This is common in Matthew. He frequently arranges material thematically rather than giving a strict chronological sequence. Like Matthew, Mark (Mk 2:23-28; 3:1) also does not explicitly say “on another Sabbath.” Luke explicitly says “another Sabbath,” while Matthew and Mark leave the interval unspecified.

15-16.x: Aware of their plot, Jesus withdraws from the area. Large crowds follow him, and he continues to heal them all. However, he warns them not to make him known. This points to the “quiet” nature of his ministry (he was not looking for a political uprising or a circus-like atmosphere); he was focused on the actual “rest” and restoration of the people. The transition from the synagogue (v.9) to the secret healings (v15-16) shows Jesus moving away from the old Jewish religious system and establishing a new way of relating to God based on his own person and power.

22-23.x: This miracle is unique because the man’s physical abilities (blindness and muteness) are attributed to a spiritual cause (demonic possession). When the crowds used the term “Son of David,” they were using a specific Messianic title. They were asking: “Could this be the Son of David, the Messiah we’ve been waiting for?”. According to Jewish tradition and prophecy (like Isaiah 35), the opening of the eyes of the blind and the unstopping of the ears of the deaf were specific “credentials” of the Messiah, however, they had doubts because they were expecting a great military leader (Jn 6:15; Acts 1:6; Lk 24:21; Dan 7:13-14; Isa 9:6-7; etc), instead Jesus was a gentle healer who would not break a “bruised reed” nor quench a "smoking flax.”(Mt 12:20). The “Son of David” title also refers to Jesus’ legal and biological lineage according to the flesh. As the firstborn of Joseph, he was entitled to the Davidic throne (Mt 1:20). However, the power to cast out a devil and heal blindness came from the Father (the Spirit) dwelling within that flesh. Jesus didn’t call another person in the Trinity to do the healing. He acted with the inherent authority of the Godhead (Mt 11:27).

25-26.x: “Jesus knew their thoughts”: although Jesus’ flesh was not omnipresent nor omniscient, his divine Spirit was. Jesus reduced the argument to its absurd conclusion: If Satan empowers Jesus to cast out demons, then Satan is fighting his own soldiers. A civil war within the demonic realm would lead to the total collapse of Satan’s power, therefore, the Pharisees’ argument is logically impossible.

Mathew 12:27: This verse shows that the Pharisees themselves were able to cast out demons by elaborate rituals, incantations, herbs, and magical formulas. In Acts 19:13-14 we see the sons of Sceva trying to cast out a demon. Unlike Jesus’ effortless command, their success was inconsistent and attributed to human techniques invoking God’s name, not Satanic power. “therefore they shall be your judges”: their own exorcists would condemn the Pharisees' reasoning; their inconsistency would be exposed by the very people they approved of, like saying: “your own side proves you wrong.”

31-32.x: To understand what this sin is, we must look at what the Pharisees just did. They witnessed the undeniable power of God (healing the blind/mute) and, rather than submitting to it, they attributed the divine power to Beelzebub (the devil). This is not a one-time slip of the tongue or a moment of doubt. It is a deliberate, persistent hardening of the heart that calls “evil” what is clearly “good,” and calls “God” what is clearly “the devil.” This sin is unpardonable, not because God refuses to forgive, but because the person has rejected the only means of forgiveness. If the Holy Spirit is the one who convicts a person of sin and reveals Jesus as Savior, and you call the Spirit “demonic,” you have cut yourself off from the only source of pardon. Now, the question is, WHY CAN YOU BLASPHEME THE SON OF MAN BUT NOT THE HOLY SPIRIT? A Trinitarian does not have a good answer, they’d typically respond with: “well, that’s what God’s Word says, so we just accept it.” or say something like: “someone never exposed to Christ’s divine power and presence might reject him in ignorance and be forgiven” and then give Saul of Tarsus as evidence in how he spoke & blasphemed against Jesus (1 Tim 1:13) because of his unbelief and ignorance, but was later forgiven (John McArthur Study Notes for Mt 12:32). Although these are decent attempts at trying to harmonize the Bible, the bottom line is that they’re teaching you can blaspheme God-the-Son, but not God-the-Holy-Spirit. If this was about “ignorance”, then blaspheming the Holy Spirit in “ignorance” should be as forgivable as blaspheming the Son in “ignorance.” But that’s not what happens here, hence it is not a satisfactory explanation. In any case, this would also undermine their doctrine of co-equality between the persons of the Godhead, as they’re obviously not treated equally here. The Oneness position shines in passages like these because it can easily differentiate between the “Son of Man” and the “Holy Spirit”(the Father, the only true God who is Spirit, Jn 4:24;17:3). You can blaspheme the “Son of Man” because it refers to the humanity of Jesus, the authentic human being begotten in Mary’s womb. The “Son of Man” is the image of the invisible God, but is not God himself. When you look at yourself in the mirror, is your reflection(image) you? Yes it is, but not really, it is simply a reflection of the real human being that you are. Likewise, the man Jesus, is the image and reflection of the Divine Spirit(Col 1:15), but he’s not actually God, he only reflects God, for God is a Spirit and He does not have bones and flesh(Jn 4:24). The man Jesus is the LAMB of God, not God-the-Lamb(Jn 1:36). The title “God-the-Son” is unbiblical, the biblical title is “Son OF God”. The Spirit glorifies the body, not the other way around(Jn 16:14). The body is useless by itself, he submits and obeys the Father unto death: “Verily, verily, I say unto you, THE SON CAN DO NOTHING OF HIMSELF, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise” (Jn 5:30 KJV). So, as a man, others could slander the “Son of Man” and call him a glutton, a winebiber, or a carpenter’s son, and still later come to realize & believe that he and the Father are one (Jn 10:30) and be forgiven. The Holy Spirit refers to the Deity. The Father is “Spirit” (Jn 4:24) and the Father is “Holy” (Jn 17:11), hence “Holy Spirit.” It simply describes the true nature of the Father. To blaspheme the Holy Spirit is to reject the very act of God’s power and presence in the world. The unforgivable sin is unbelief in God, willfully suppressing the truth: “For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). “neither in this world, neither in the world to come”: Since there is no Biblical support for Purgatory, Romanism attempts to teach that “the world to come” refers to Purgatory. However, the only way to harmonize the entire Bible is by having “the world to come” to mean either the Millennial Kingdom or the Eternal Age following Judgement Day.

38-40.x: The religious leaders wanted a spectacular “on-demand” miracle (like fire from heaven) to satisfy their skepticism. Jesus refuses for two reasons: (1) The Motive: Seeking a sign when God has already clearly spoken (through the healings earlier in the chapter) is a sign of a hardened, “adulterous” heart. (2) The Ultimate Sign: Jesus points them to the Resurrection. Just as Jonah was “entombed” in this great fish and then “resurrected” to preach to Nineveh, Jesus would be buried and rise again. This is the only sign that they will be given due to the hardness of their hearts. Likewise today, there is plenty of information regarding the historicity of Jesus’ life, death, & resurrection. For many, that will be the only sign in their lives. Notice how Jesus takes Jonah’s account as actual history. Our faith revolves around Jesus’ resurrection, not on the OT stories. If Jesus’ resurrection is true (as all the evidence suggests it actually happened), then anything the person with power over life says must be taken seriously. For more on the actual literary, archaeological, and circumstantial evidence on the resurrection of Jesus, read “The Case For Christ” by Lee Strobel.

41-42.x: Jesus then uses two Gentile examples to shame the Jewish leadership: (1) The Men of Niniveh: They were heathens, yet they repented at the simple preaching of Jonah. Jesus says: “behold, a greater than Jonas is here.” (2) The Queen of the South: She traveled a vast distance to hear the wisdom of Solomon. Jesus says: “behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” The point is that, if pagans could recognize God’s wisdom and call to repentance in flawed men like Jonah and Solomon, the Pharisees are without excuse for rejecting the very Son of God standing in their presence. Jesus is greater than the temple (v.6), the prophet Jonah, and the wise King Solomon. He and his message are greater than (and are the fulfillment of) the three greatest institutions in Israel: priest, prophet, and king. “The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment.. And shall condemn it”: Scripture shows that believers will participate in judgement: (1) “Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world? and if the world shall be judged by you, are ye unworthy to judge the smallest matters?” (1 Cor 6:2-3 KJV); (2) “If we suffer, we shall also reign with him...” (2 Tim 2:12 KJV); (3) “And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them...” (Rev 20:4 KJV); (4) “...ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” (Mt 19:28 KJV); (5) “...judgment was given to the saints of the most High...” (Dan 7:22 KJV); etc.

43-45.x: “dry places”: refers to a “desert” (NLT), “arid places” (BSB), or “waterless places” (LSB). In ancient Jewish thought, demons were often associated with desolate wilderness or desert areas. These are dry, barren “uninhabitable” zones where spirits roam restlessly without a host. Metaphorically speaking, water symbolizes life, blessing, and the Holy Spirit in Scripture (Jn 7:38-39). A “waterless place” is the complete opposite: dry, lifeless spots with no rest or “home.” The evil spirit seeks a living person (who is mostly water) to inhabit, like a thirsty traveler in a desert. Without one, it finds no satisfaction. Here, Jesus describes a person who has undergone a superficial reformation. The “unclean spirit” (demon) has left, perhaps because the person started following religious rules or cleaned up their outward behavior. The house is “swept and garnished.” It looks clean, orderly, and religious on the outside. However, the house is “empty.” While the “bad” has been removed, nothing “good” has moved in to take its place. And because there is no “New Tenant” (the Holy Spirit) protecting the house, the original spirit returns with seven others. The person ends up in a much worse spiritual condition than before. If you focus only on removing the bad (the “don’ts” of the Law), you leave yourself empty. The only safety is in being occupied by the “Stronger Man” (v.29). The goal of the spiritual life is not an “empty” house of perfect rule-following, but a “full” house where God Himself dwells.

46-50.x: In the parallel passage of Mark, we see that Jesus’ family was trying to do an intervention: “And when his friends heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself.” (Mk 3:21 KJV). They thought Jesus was out of his mind, and wanted to “lay hold of him.” Then the same scene occurs when his family makes the move in Mk 3:31-35 & Mt 12:46-50. His family was not just casually visiting - they were trying to intervene and restrain him because they thought something was wrong. “For neither did his brethren believe in him.” (Jn 7:5 KJV) - at this point in his ministry, his brothers did not believe. But, instead of going out immediately, Jesus uses the moment to redefine family: “whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.” This passage does not mean that Jesus rejected his biological family entirely, but that, at that moment, his family did not fully understand his mission & Jesus prioritized obedience to the Father above all. For Jesus, the Spiritual Family takes precedence over the Biological Family. In fact, he never ever mentions Mary as “mother.”; he only calls her “woman.” The omission of Jesus’ earthly father, Joseph, may suggest that he had already died at this point.

The CT omits Matthew 12:47: “Then ONE SAID UNTO HIM, Behold, thy mother and thy brethren stand without, desiring to speak with thee” KJV. In this verse, someone tells Jesus that his family is trying to speak with him. In verse 48, Jesus responds to this person: “But he answered and SAID UNTO HIM THAT TOLD HIM, Who is my mother? and who are my brethren?” KJV. In translations based on the CT, like the ESV and RSV, you don’t know who Jesus is replying to. Another Matthew example is Matthew 19:17, where translations based on the CT read like: “Why do you ask me ABOUT WHAT IS GOOD? There is only one who is good” (ESV), even when all the parallel passages read like: “Why do you CALL ME GOOD? No one is good except God alone” (Mk 10:18 ESV; Lk 18:19 ESV). Translations based on the TR/MT accurately render Matthew 19:17: “Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God” (KJV) and accurately harmonizes with the rest of Scripture (Mk 10:18; Lk 18:19) and the immediate Biblical context. By following only two manuscripts from Alexandria, Egypt simply because they’re the oldest, the CT introduces new errors into Scripture. And recall that even those two manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) differ among themselves. For example, in Matthew alone: in Mt 1:25, Sinaiticus includes “her firstborn son” like the TR, while Vaticanus omits “firstborn,” or in Mt 27:49, where Sinaiticus includes a sentence about a spear piercing Jesus (matching Jn 19:34), but Vaticanus omits it.

Since Catholicism teaches that Mary is a perpetual virgin, these brothers cannot be biological siblings, but cousins, or sons of a previous marriage of Joseph. First, Jesus is called the “firstborn” (Lk 2:7), meaning there were “later-born” children. Second, Jesus has to be the older brother, otherwise he would not have a royal claim to the Davidic line. Third, the Greek language has a specific word for “cousin” (anepsios), which is used in Col 4:10. If Matthew intended to say cousins, he had a specific word available. Instead, he uses adelphos, the standard word for a brother. Likewise, Luke also describes Jesus as having brothers (Lk 8:19-21), even when he constantly uses the word “syngenēs”, which means “relative” (Lk 1:36, 58). Fourth, throughout the gospels, these individuals are almost always grouped with Mary (as seen in v.46). In the ancient Near East, it would be highly unusual for a group of cousins to be constantly traveling and living with their aunt as a single nuclear unit. Fifth, in Mt 13:55-56, the people of Nazareth name his brothers (James, Joses, Simon, and Judas) and mention his “sisters.” They speak of them as part of the immediate household of the carpenter, as they were his hometown neighbors. Lastly (at least for this section): without a preconceived theological requirement to see Mary as a perpetual virgin, the most natural reading of the Greek text is that these are the younger siblings of Jesus. It is essential that Jesus Christ was truly and fully human—the Son—because, as Scripture teaches, “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22 KJV). In order to redeem humanity, He had to share in our nature and condition. As it is written, He was “made of a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4:4 KJV), entering fully into the human experience. At the same time, all judgment has been entrusted to Him: “For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son” (John 5:22 KJV). Therefore, it was fitting that He should experience the realities of human life, so that His judgment would be both just and compassionate. Scripture affirms this, saying, “For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15 KJV). His having a real mother and real siblings further confirms His genuine humanity. He did not merely appear human, but truly lived as one of us, yet without sin, demonstrating that obedience to God in the flesh is possible and providing a perfect basis for both our redemption and His righteous judgment.
